items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to

Content:
[MATH: \cos\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2},
\qquad -\pi \leq x < \pi.]

Content:
Notice that the equation contains a transformed cosine function.

Content:
We know that the general solution to the elementary equation [MATH: \cos{X} = \dfrac{1}{2}] is given by

Content:
[MATH: X|= (π)/(3) + 2nπ,|X|= (5π)/(3) + 2nπ,]

Content:
where [MATH: n] is assumed to be any integer.

Content:
To find the general solution of the transformed cosine equation, we replace [MATH: X] with the input of the cosine function, which is [MATH: x + \dfrac{\pi}{3}] in this case. This gives the general solution

Content:
[MATH: x+\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi, \qquad\qquad x+\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{5\pi}{3}+ 2n\pi.]

Content:
We now solve the above two equations for [MATH: x,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x|= 2nπ|x|= (4π)/(3) + 2nπ; x|= (4π)/(3) + (6nπ)/(3); x|= (2π(2 + 3n))/(3)]

Content:
Now, we set [MATH: n = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \ldots] until we have generated all solutions in the domain [MATH: -\pi \leq x < \pi.]

Content:
- Setting [MATH: n=0] gives [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: x=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}.] We reject the solution [MATH: \dfrac{4\pi}{3}] since it lies outside the domain of interest.
- Setting [MATH: n=-1] gives [MATH: x=-2\pi] and [MATH: x=-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}.] We reject the solution [MATH: -2\pi] since it lies outside the domain of interest.

Content:
All other values of [MATH: n] generate solutions outside the domain [MATH: -\pi \leq x < \pi.] So, the solutions [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] (written in ascending order) are

Content:
[MATH: x_1 = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\qquad x_2 = 0.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is given by

[MATH: 2x|= (π)/(4) + 2nπ,|2x|= (7π)/(4) + 2nπ.]

Solving our two equations for [MATH: x] gives the following:

[MATH: x|= (π)/(8) + nπ|x|= (7π)/(8) + nπ; x|= (π)/(8) + (8nπ)/(8)|x|= (7π)/(8) + (8nπ)/(8); x|= ((8n + 1)π)/(8)|x|= ((8n + 7)π)/(8)]

We set [MATH: n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots,] until we have generated all solutions in the domain [MATH: 0 \leq x \lt 2\pi.]

  • Setting [MATH: n=0] gives [MATH: x=\dfrac{\pi}{8}] and [MATH: x=\dfrac{7\pi}{8}.]

  • Setting [MATH: n=1] gives [MATH: x=\dfrac{9\pi}{8}] and [MATH: x=\dfrac{15\pi}{8}.]

All other values of [MATH: n] generate solutions outside the domain [MATH: 0 \leq x \lt 2\pi.] So, the solutions [MATH: x_1, x_2, x_3] and [MATH: x_4] (written in ascending order) are [MATH: x = \dfrac{\pi}{8}, \, \dfrac{7\pi}{8}, \, \dfrac{9\pi}{8}, \, \dfrac{15\pi}{8}.]

Finally,

[MATH: x_2\cdot x_3 = \dfrac{7\pi}{8} \cdot \dfrac{9\pi}{8} = \dfrac{63\pi^2}{64}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows: [MATH: − 2sqrt(3)\cos (2x + 60^{∘}) − 3|= 0; − 2sqrt(3)\cos (2x + 60^{∘})|= 3; \cos (2x + 60^{∘})|= − (3)/(2sqrt(3)); \cos (2x + 60^{∘})|= − (sqrt(3))/(2)]

We will find the general solution to the equation and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is

[MATH: 2x + 60^{∘}|= 150^{∘} + n ⋅ 360^{∘},|2x + 60^{∘}|= 210^{∘} + n ⋅ 360^{∘}.]

Solving the two equations above for [MATH: x] gives the following:

[MATH: 2x|= 150^{∘} − 60^{∘} + n ⋅ 360^{∘}|2x|= 210^{∘} − 60^{∘} + n ⋅ 360^{∘}; 2x|= 90^{∘} + n ⋅ 360^{∘}|2x|= 150^{∘} + n ⋅ 360^{∘}; x|= 45^{∘} + n ⋅ 180^{∘}|x|= 75^{∘} + n ⋅ 180^{∘}]

We set [MATH: n=0, \pm 1, \pm 2,\ldots] until we have generated all solutions in the domain [MATH: 0^\circ \leq x \lt 360^\circ.]

  • Setting [MATH: n=0] gives [MATH: x=45^\circ] and [MATH: x=75^\circ.]

  • Setting [MATH: n=1] gives [MATH: x=225^\circ] and [MATH: x=255^\circ.]

All other values of [MATH: n] generate solutions outside the domain [MATH: 0^\circ \leq x \lt 360^\circ.] So, the solutions [MATH: x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4] (written in ascending order) are

[MATH: x_1 = 45^\circ,\quad x_2 = 75^\circ,\quad x_3 = 225^\circ,\quad x_4= 255^\circ .]
